abstract: Synaptic plasticity is a fundamental mechanism underlying learning and memory. Most excitatory synapses reside on dendritic spines, which undergo both functional and structural changes. These two forms of plasticity are typically tightly coupled: spines enlarge during synaptic strengthening (long-term potentiation, LTP) and shrink during synaptic weakening (long-term depression, LTD). While this coupling is well established for NMDA receptor (NMDAR)-dependent LTD, there are conflicting reports concerning whether spine shrinkage is coupled with metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR)-dependent LTD. To investigate the source of these conflicting results, we induced mGluR-LTD with the mGluR1/5 agonist DHPG in organotypic rat hippocampal slice cultures and monitored changes in spine morphology and calcium transients in CA1 pyramidal neurons expressing DsRed2 and GCaMP6. We found that mGluR activation is accompanied by long-term spine shrinkage only under conditions of elevated hippocampal neuronal activity. This form of plasticity, mGluR-induced neuronal activity-dependent structural LTD (MIND-sLTD), requires mGluR1/5 activation and de novo protein synthesis, but not NMDAR signaling. Persistent structural changes occur only when neuronal activity coincides temporally with mGluR activation. MIND-sLTD also occurs at individual synapses: mGluR activation induces persistent single-spine shrinkage only when synchronized with two-photon glutamate uncaging, independently of NMDARs. These findings identify a novel form of structural plasticity and suggest a coincidence-detection mechanism that integrates mGluR signaling with synaptic activity to consolidate long-term spine remodeling.
